title: The lab
plain: A small Python toolbox starts the Minecraft server with no game window, sends it commands, resets it, shuts it down and times every step.
why: Every experiment after this one needs a server we can start and wipe from a script, safely.
done_when: A script can boot, command, reset and stop the server, and no server is left running afterwards.

title: Talking to the server
plain: The toolbox learns the server's remote-command language (RCON) so a script can type commands into the server.
why: Without it nothing can place blocks or generate chunks on purpose.
done_when: A script can log in and get an answer back, and a wrong password is refused.

title: Build RCON messages
plain: Turn a command into the exact bytes the server expects, and turn the server's bytes back into text.
why: A single wrong byte and the server ignores us, so the format is checked first against the written spec.
done_when: The login and command messages come out byte for byte as the spec says.

title: RCON client on a fake server
plain: A client logs in, sends commands and joins long answers, tested against a pretend server that we control.
why: We can test refusals and very long answers instantly, without waiting 20 seconds for the real game.
done_when: A wrong password is refused and a reply over 4096 bytes arrives whole.

title: Running the server
plain: The toolbox starts a private copy of the server, waits until it says it is ready, resets the world and always shuts it down.
why: A reset in about 20 seconds makes every experiment start from the same empty world.
done_when: Boot, reset and stop all work, each is timed, and no Java process is left behind.

title: Private server copy
plain: Copy the server jar and settings into a scratch folder, turn the remote commands on with a random password and a free port, and never touch the original folder.
why: The original server folder stays exactly as it is, and each copy can run beside another.
done_when: The copy has RCON on, a long random password and its own port, and the original files are unchanged.

title: Stop politely, then force
plain: Ask a program to stop, wait a set time, and kill it if it ignores us.
why: A stuck server would otherwise sit on our small memory for good.
done_when: A stubborn test program is gone within the time limit.

title: Start and wait for Done
plain: Start the server with a 1 GB limit and no window, and wait until its log says Done.
why: This is the first moment the server can be used, and the time to get there is a number we report.
done_when: The server prints Done within 60 seconds and answers the list command.

title: Reset to an empty world
plain: Stop the server, delete its world, and start it again so nothing from before survives.
why: Every experiment must start from the same blank world or its numbers mean nothing.
done_when: A block placed before the reset is gone after it, and no Java process is left running.

title: Time and memory of the lab
plain: Measure how long boot and reset take and the most memory the server uses, and save the numbers.
why: The earlier memory number was one sample, and the plan for how many servers to run at once depends on the peak.
done_when: A results file holds boot seconds, reset seconds and the peak memory in megabytes.

title: No game files in our repo
plain: A check walks the whole repository and fails if it finds the server program, a world file or a server settings file.
why: The game files belong to someone else, so none may ever be committed.
done_when: The check passes on the repo and fails on a copy that has a jar or a region file in it.

title: Many worlds per gigabyte
plain: Memory is the limit, so the lab measures which way of making many fresh worlds gives the most worlds per minute for each gigabyte: several ordinary servers, or many worlds inside one game process the way speedrunners do.
why: The order experiment needs dozens of fresh worlds, and the cheaper way to get them saves hours; this is a measured choice and not a belief.
done_when: Both ways have saved numbers (or a stated reason one could not run), and a choice file names the winner.

title: Several ordinary servers
plain: Run one, two and three of our private servers at once, resetting each over and over for three minutes, and count fresh worlds per minute and memory per world.
why: This is the baseline route and needs nothing new to be downloaded.
done_when: The results file holds worlds per minute, total memory and memory per world for one, two and three servers.

title: What is installed already
plain: List, without downloading or changing anything, whether the owner's game folder already holds a 1.16.1 client, the Fabric mod loader, a mods folder and the right Java.
why: Whether the many-worlds route can start at all depends on this, and the answer is read, not remembered.
done_when: The results file says found or missing for each item, and the game folder is unchanged.

title: Many worlds in one game
plain: Measure worlds per minute and memory per world with the speedrunner mods that prepare several worlds inside one game process; it downloads nothing until the owner approves the file list, and otherwise records exactly why it is blocked.
why: Several worlds sharing one process could beat several servers per gigabyte, but this route needs a game window and downloads, so it must not hold anything else up.
done_when: The results file holds the measured numbers, or says blocked with the reason.

title: Choose the route
plain: Read the saved numbers and pick the route with more worlds per minute for each gigabyte, falling back to ordinary servers whenever the other route is missing or blocked.
why: One file tells every later experiment which route and how many workers to use.
done_when: Made-up numbers give the right winner, a blocked or missing route falls back to ordinary servers, and the real choice file is saved.

title: Run jobs on several workers
plain: Hand a list of build orders to the chosen workers, never more than three servers at once, and get the results back in the order the jobs were given.
why: The order experiment gets its dozens of worlds faster, and it can use either route without being rewritten.
done_when: With pretend workers the results come back in job order, one worker failing is reported, and asking for four servers is refused.

title: The chunk reader
plain: A Python reader opens the world files the server saved and says which block sits at any position.
why: The experiments compare blocks, so the reader must be right before any number is believed.
done_when: The reader returns exactly the blocks we placed with commands on a live server.

title: Reading one region file
plain: The reader learns to open a region file, unpack the data format and turn a slice of a chunk into block names.
why: These are the steps every later read depends on.
done_when: Hand-built region files and slices read back exactly.

title: Read the NBT format
plain: Read the nested data format (NBT) the game saves chunks in: named values, lists and arrays of numbers.
why: Everything in a world file is stored in this format.
done_when: A hand-built sample with a compound, a list and a long array reads back exactly.

title: Open a region file
plain: A region file holds up to 1024 chunks; find which are present and unpack one chunk's bytes.
why: This is how we know which chunks the server has built.
done_when: A made-up region file with two chunks lists exactly those two and unpacks one.

title: Unpack a 16-block slice
plain: Turn one slice of a chunk (a palette of block names plus packed numbers) into 4096 block names, using the 1.16 packing where numbers never straddle two values.
why: Version 1.16 changed the packing, and the old layout silently gives wrong blocks.
done_when: Hand-packed slices with 5-bit and 6-bit entries unpack to the exact blocks.

title: Block at any position
plain: Ask for the block at x, y, z, including negative coordinates, plus a chunk's build status, with missing chunks answering nothing.
why: Negative positions are where reading mistakes hide, and the build status shows if a chunk is finished.
done_when: Positions in chunk minus one and at slice edges read right, and a missing chunk answers none.

title: Using the reader
plain: The reader reads a whole box of blocks, and is proven on the live server.
why: A reader is only trusted after it reads back what the game itself wrote.
done_when: A box fingerprint is stable and five placed blocks are read back right.

title: Read a box of blocks
plain: Read every block in a box and fingerprint it, so two boxes can be compared quickly.
why: The order experiment compares boxes of blocks and a fingerprint tells at once if they match.
done_when: The same box read twice gives the same fingerprint, and one changed block changes it.

title: Proof on the live server
plain: Place five known blocks with commands, save, stop, and check the reader finds every one of them.
why: This is the only proof that the reader sees what the game really wrote.
done_when: All five placed blocks, including a negative position and a slice edge, are read back right.

title: The next-chunk lever
plain: Find out whether anything the player does before a chunk is built changes what that chunk holds, starting with the order the chunks are built in.
why: This is goal one: a move made before a chunk exists that changes the chunk, measured on the real game.
done_when: A results file says, with counts, whether building order or a player edit changed any block, and whether it moved diamonds.

title: Build chunks and compare them
plain: The tools, the one-at-a-time building, the first pair and the wider search over orders.
why: This is the order experiment itself, from smallest step to widest search.
done_when: Every order is built, compared and counted, and the control is zero.

title: Measuring tools
plain: Two small tools: one finds every block that differs between two builds, the other counts ores.
why: Every claim in this branch is a count made by these tools.
done_when: Both tools give the right counts on hand-made examples.

title: Find differing blocks
plain: Compare two block maps and list every position whose block changed, appeared or vanished.
why: Zero or not zero differing blocks decides the whole order question.
done_when: Three planted differences are found and identical maps give an empty list.

title: Count the ores
plain: Count diamond, iron, coal, gold, lapis, redstone and emerald blocks in a box, chunk by chunk.
why: The aim is more diamond, so diamond must be counted per chunk.
done_when: A hand-made box with known ores gives the exact counts per chunk.

title: Building chunks one at a time
plain: The lab builds chosen chunks one after another, far from the world spawn, and waits for each to finish before asking for the next.
why: If two chunks are built at once the order is not ours, so the order experiment would mean nothing.
done_when: Chunks come out in the order we gave, and a neighbour of a finished chunk is still half built.

title: Wait until a chunk is built
plain: Ask the server to hold a chunk loaded, then keep asking whether bedrock is there until the answer is yes or time runs out.
why: This is how one chunk is finished before the next is requested.
done_when: A pretend server that says not yet three times and then yes makes it wait, and a timeout is reported.

title: Spawn is not in the way
plain: The server builds a big area around spawn at start; check that a chunk thousands of blocks away is not built until we ask.
why: If spawn already built our test chunks, the order would be the server's and not ours.
done_when: The far chunk is absent from the saved files before we ask and finished after.

title: A neighbour is only half built
plain: Build one chunk, then read the status of its neighbour in the saved files.
why: Building a chunk makes the neighbours partly, which is why order could matter.
done_when: The neighbour exists but its status is not full.

title: Run one build order
plain: Given a list of chunks, build them in exactly that order on a fresh world and return the blocks of the whole area.
why: Everything after this is a comparison of such runs.
done_when: A run of two chunks returns both chunks as finished with the full box of blocks.

title: The first pair
plain: The smallest honest experiment: one pair of neighbour chunks built A then B and B then A, with a control that repeats one order.
why: One pair is cheap, and the control says whether a difference could be noise.
done_when: The control shows zero differing blocks, and the pair has an exact count.

title: Same order twice
plain: Build A then B twice on fresh worlds and count the differing blocks; this must be zero or the test is too noisy to use.
why: If the same order differs from itself, nothing later can be trusted; if so, mask the moving water and lava and run it again before going on.
done_when: The count is zero, or the leftover differences are listed and masked.

title: A then B against B then A
plain: Build the pair in both orders and count the differing blocks; zero means this pair has no lever, and more pairs are tried next.
why: Differing blocks here would be the first proof that building order changes a chunk.
done_when: The results file holds the exact count of differing blocks and where they are.

title: More orders and places
plain: If the pair showed nothing, widen the search: every order of four chunks in a square, then more squares far apart.
why: One pair at one place proves little; all 24 orders at three places is a fair test of the order idea.
done_when: Every order of every square is tallied, and the number of differing blocks is exact, even if zero.

title: List the 24 orders
plain: Write down every order in which four chunks of a square can be built, and start the empty not-run table that the later runs fill in.
why: The experiment must not miss or repeat an order, and an unfilled table must read as not run.
done_when: There are 24 orders, all different, each with the four chunks, and the starter table says not run.

title: All 24 orders, first square
plain: Build the square in all 24 orders, compare each with the first, and tally the ores per chunk for every order.
why: This is the main table: how many blocks and how many diamonds change with the order.
done_when: The results file has 24 rows with differing-block counts and ore counts.

title: Two more squares
plain: Repeat all 24 orders on two other squares far from the first.
why: A lever that exists only at one place would not help a speedrun.
done_when: The results file holds 48 more rows from two other squares.

title: What to do with the answer
plain: The player-edit lever, the aim at diamonds and the verdict that closes goal one.
why: These steps turn the measured counts into an answer, whichever way they came out.
done_when: The edit lever is tested, the aim says aimed or no lever, and the verdict is written.

title: The player edit lever
plain: If the order did nothing, test the other lever: blocks the player broke or placed in a finished chunk before its neighbour is built.
why: A player can do this in the real game, so it is the next place to look.
done_when: Cells outside the edit are counted as changed or not, against a no-edit control.

title: Edit commands
plain: Turn a list of blocks to break or place into server commands that only touch finished, loaded chunks.
why: A command into an unloaded chunk would build it early and spoil the order.
done_when: The commands are right for a break and a place, and one into an unloaded chunk is refused.

title: Edit then build the neighbour
plain: Build chunk A, break blocks near its edge, build chunk B, and count changed cells outside the edit against a run with no edit.
why: Changed cells outside the edit would mean the player shaped the next chunk.
done_when: The results file holds the count of changed cells outside the edit and where they are.

title: Aiming at diamonds
plain: Only if something differed: find the order that gives a chosen chunk the most diamonds, and check it holds up; if nothing differed, these steps must say no lever.
why: This is the owner's sketch: a move before the chunk is built that gives it more diamond.
done_when: The result says aimed with a repeatable gain, or says no lever.

title: Pick the best order
plain: Given a table of orders and diamond counts, pick the order with the most diamonds in the target chunk, or say there is no lever when all counts are equal.
why: Both answers must be correct, because a zero result is a result.
done_when: A table with a clear best picks it, and an all-equal table answers no lever.

title: Aim on the real table
plain: Run the picker on the real tables and save the answer, with the average over all orders next to it.
why: The gain only means something against the average order.
done_when: The file says aimed with the best count and the average, or says no lever.

title: Repeat the best order
plain: Build the chosen order twice on fresh worlds; the diamond count must match the table both times, or the difference was noise.
why: A gain that does not repeat is not a gain.
done_when: Both repeats give the table's count, or the file says nothing to repeat.

title: Does it work on a new place
plain: Take the rule found on the first squares and try it on a square it never saw, against that square's average.
why: A rule that only works where it was found cannot be used in a run.
done_when: The rule's diamonds beat the average at the new square, or the file says it did not.

title: The verdict
plain: One file states what is alive and what is dead for goal one, with every claim tied to its limits.
why: A no must be as exact as a yes, and no solver can answer every question about Minecraft, so each claim says its bound.
done_when: The verdict file matches the result files and names the next route for anything dead.

title: Write the verdict
plain: Turn the result files into plain statements that each name the seed, area, height and number of orders, say not run for missing files, and give the next route for a dead lever.
why: Every claim then carries its own bound.
done_when: Made-up result files give the right alive, dead and not-run statements with the bounds and a reroute.

title: Verdict on the real results
plain: Run the verdict writer on the real result files and save the file the website reads.
why: This is the single answer to goal one.
done_when: The saved verdict repeats the exact counts in the result files.

title: The fastest run
plain: Read real seed 7 terrain with the new reader, then race the round 1 planner against the round 1 plain search on it in game ticks; playing the route in the real game with a bot is a later round.
why: This is goal two: a fastest route on the real map, beating a simple baseline in game ticks.
done_when: On the real map the planner finishes in fewer ticks than the plain search, with numbers saved.

title: Real terrain as a grid
plain: The real world, 3D, is flattened into the flat grid the solver already understands, and checked against the live game.
why: The solver and the real game meet here, so a mistake here ruins every route.
done_when: A real area of seed 7 is a grid file, and sampled squares match the live server.

title: The flat file both languages agree on
plain: Python flattens the terrain and writes a grid file, and Rust reads the very same bytes back.
why: Python writes and Rust reads, so one shared sample stops them drifting apart.
done_when: The bytes Python writes equal the saved sample, and Rust reads the sample's squares correctly.

title: Flatten columns
plain: Turn each column of blocks into one square: tree if a log stands there, water, iron if ore is within six blocks below, a stone wall if the ground jumps two blocks, else open ground.
why: The solver is flat, so this rule is a stated model, and it is tested so it can be changed.
done_when: A made-up landscape gives the expected tree, water, iron, wall and open squares.

title: Write the grid file
plain: Write the squares in the byte format the Rust grid reads, and keep one tiny sample file both languages must agree on.
why: Python writes and Rust reads, so one shared sample stops them drifting apart.
done_when: The bytes Python writes equal the saved sample file, byte for byte.

title: Rust reads the grid
plain: The round 1 Rust grid reader loads the shared sample file and gives the right size and squares; no new Rust library is needed.
why: If Python and Rust ever disagree about the file, this test fails first.
done_when: Loading the shared sample gives the right size and the right squares.

title: Area export script
plain: A script turns a box of real blocks into a grid file using the flattening rule and the grid writer, with the area (64 by 64 squares around spawn) written down in one place.
why: The export logic is checked on made-up blocks before it ever touches the real world.
done_when: A made-up box of blocks becomes the expected grid bytes.

title: Export a real seed 7 area
plain: Build an area of the real seed 7 world, read it, and save it as a grid; it must have open ground, a tree, stone and iron, or the area is widened.
why: This is the real map the race is run on.
done_when: The grid file exists and contains a start square, a tree, stone and iron.

title: Check squares on the live server
plain: Pick random squares from the grid and ask the running server what block is really there.
why: This tests the flattening rule against the game, not against our idea of it.
done_when: Every sampled square agrees with the live server.

title: The race on real terrain
plain: The round 1 planner races the round 1 plain move-counting search on the real grid, from one start and then from many starts.
why: Beating a fair simple rival, with the control, is the proof the planner is any good.
done_when: The planner is never slower, and its wins are counted.

title: Pick a start and a finish
plain: Choose a start square near the middle and a finish square next to the nearest iron, on any grid, so every race uses the same rule.
why: Fixed rules for start and finish keep the race fair and repeatable.
done_when: On a hand-made grid the start and the finish are the squares worked out on paper.

title: Wall trap map
plain: On a map with a short wall and a long way round, the round 1 plain search digs the wall and the planner walks round in fewer ticks.
why: This shows on a small map exactly why planning in ticks beats counting moves.
done_when: The planner's ticks are lower than the plain search's on the trap map.

title: Race on seed 7
plain: Run both on the real seed 7 grid from one start and save the ticks of each.
why: This is the first real result for goal two.
done_when: The planner's ticks are not above the rival's, and the file records both numbers.

title: Race from many starts
plain: Repeat the race from twenty different start squares and count the wins, ties and losses.
why: One start can be luck; twenty show if the planner really is faster.
done_when: Zero losses in twenty starts, with the number of strict wins saved.

title: The website shows round 2
plain: A web page shows the round 2 goals in plain words and the experiment's numbers, and says not run yet for anything not measured.
why: The owner watches the project here, and the numbers must be the real ones.
done_when: The page at http://127.0.0.1:7740/r2.html shows every goal and the real experiment numbers.

title: Build the round 2 data
plain: A script merges the fellows' plain-English files for round 2 with each goal's status into one data file.
why: The page reads one file, the same way round 1 does.
done_when: Goals from two chart files are merged by id and a goal without a status shows pending.

title: Pull in the experiment numbers
plain: The same script copies the numbers from the result files into the data file, and a missing file is marked not run, never zero.
why: A missing result shown as zero would look like a finding.
done_when: With no result files every number says not run, and with files the counts are copied exactly.

title: The round 2 page
plain: A page draws a card for every goal and one bar for every build order showing its differing-block count.
why: A bar chart of counts per order is the picture of the experiment.
done_when: The page reads the data file and has a card hook per goal and a bar hook per order.

title: Serve the page
plain: The existing local web server returns the round 2 page at its address.
why: The owner opens it in a browser, so it must load.
done_when: A request to the page on a free local port returns it.

title: Link from the main page
plain: The round 1 page gets one link to the round 2 page.
why: One door between the two pages.
done_when: The main page contains a link to r2.html.
